title: Why Taps Drip From the Spout (Compression Valve Mechanics)
description: When a traditional compression tap continues dripping after you turn it off, the problem lies inside the valve assembly. Water supply pressure constantly pushes against the valve. Turning the handle drives a rubber washer down onto a raised brass rim called the valve seat to block the flow. Over time, friction, mineral deposits, and over-tightening deform the washer or erode the brass seat. If you replace the rubber washer but the dripping continues, inspect the brass seat for pitting or corrosion. A seat dressing tool or replacement seat inserts can restore a smooth sealing surface. Have you encountered pitted tap seats during maintenance?

visual_story: The visual focuses on a cross-sectional cutaway of a compression tap valve assembly. Viewers can directly observe the mechanical relationship between the rubber washer and the internal brass valve seat. The visual demonstrates where the sealing failure occurs: a grooved rubber washer failing to make flush contact against the metal seat under water pressure. By showing the internal mechanics, the image enables viewers to understand why tightening a worn tap harder damages the washer further rather than stopping the leak.

on_image_text.hook: A DRIPPING TAP IS USUALLY A SEALING ISSUE
on_image_text.explanation: Water leaks past the spout when the washer can no longer form a flat seal against the internal valve seat.
on_image_text.callout: Worn Rubber Washer vs Internal Valve Seat
on_image_text.takeaway: Replace the washer first; if dripping persists, re-face or replace the valve seat.
